claims.claim: Thomas Midgley Jr., working for General Motors, first discovered tetraethyl lead's effectiveness as an anti-knock agent on December 9, 1921.
claims.episode_span: Thomas Midgley Jr. was working in a Dayton, Ohio laboratory on December 9, 1921 when he first demonstrated that a few drops of tetraethyl lead in a test engine eliminated the sharp metallic ping
claims.supporting_quote: Thomas Midgley Jr. , who was working for the U.S. corporation General Motors , was the first to discover its effectiveness as a knock inhibitor on December 9, 1921

claims.claim: Tetraethyl lead was first synthesized in 1853, decades before its use as a fuel additive.
claims.episode_span: tetraethyl lead, a little-known organic compound first synthesized in 1853, worked dramatically at concentrations as low as one part per thousand
claims.supporting_quote: TEL was first synthesized by German chemist Carl Jacob Löwig in 1853

claims.claim: After refinery worker deaths, the U.S. Public Health Service convened a conference on tetraethyl lead in 1925 and TEL sales were voluntarily suspended for a year for a hazard assessment.
claims.episode_span: in 1925 a conference convened by the Surgeon General heard testimony that workers at the Bayway refinery had died after inhaling tetraethyl lead fumes
claims.supporting_quote: To settle the issue, the U.S. Public Health Service conducted a conference in 1925, and the sales of TEL were voluntarily suspended for one year to conduct a hazard assessment

claims.claim: In 1973 the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency issued regulations phasing down the lead content of gasoline in annual steps.
claims.episode_span: in 1973 the agency announced a phased reduction schedule tied to the introduction of catalytic converters, which were poisoned by lead
claims.supporting_quote: In the U.S. in 1973, the United States Environmental Protection Agency issued regulations to reduce the lead content of leaded gasoline over a series of annual phases

claims.claim: Leaded gasoline was banned for on-road vehicles in the United States effective January 1, 1996 under the Clean Air Act.
claims.episode_span: Leaded gasoline was fully banned for on-road use in the United States by 1996.
claims.supporting_quote: From 1 January 1996, the U.S. Clean Air Act banned the sale of leaded fuel for use in on-road vehicles

claims.claim: In the 1970s Herbert Needleman found that higher lead levels in children were correlated with decreased cognitive/school performance.
claims.episode_span: Longitudinal studies begun in the 1970s by Herbert Needleman at Harvard and later replicated in multiple countries showed consistent dose-dependent reductions in IQ
claims.supporting_quote: In the 1970s, Herbert Needleman found that higher lead levels in children were correlated with decreased school performance

claims.claim: Mean U.S. blood-lead levels fell dramatically during and after the tetraethyl-lead phaseout, from 16 micrograms per deciliter in 1976 to about 3 in 1991 (roughly an 80 percent drop by 1991, continuing thereafter).
claims.episode_span: Blood-lead levels in U.S. children fell more than 90 percent between 1976 and 2010
claims.supporting_quote: For the entire US population, during and after the TEL phaseout, the mean blood lead level dropped from 16 μg/dL in 1976 to only 3 μg/dL in 1991
